claim: The study sequenced at high coverage (90X) the whole genome of 81 semi-supercentenarians and supercentenarians [105+/110+] with mean age 106.6 ± 1.6.
source: In this study, we sequenced at high coverage (90X) the whole genome of 81 semi-supercentenarians and supercentenarians [105+/110+] (mean age: 106.6 ± 1.6) and of 36 healthy unrelated geographically matched controls (mean age 68.0 ± 5.9) recruited in Italy.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the sequencing coverage, sample size, and mean age of the 105+/110+ cohort.

claim: The study sequenced 36 healthy unrelated geographically matched controls with mean age 68.0 ± 5.9.
source: In this study, we sequenced at high coverage (90X) the whole genome of 81 semi-supercentenarians and supercentenarians [105+/110+] (mean age: 106.6 ± 1.6) and of 36 healthy unrelated geographically matched controls (mean age 68.0 ± 5.9) recruited in Italy.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the sample size and mean age of the control cohort.

claim: 105+/110+ individuals are characterized by a peculiar genetic background associated with efficient DNA repair mechanisms.
source: The results showed that 105+/110+ are characterized by a peculiar genetic background associated with efficient DNA repair mechanisms, as evidenced by both germline data (common and rare variants) and somatic mutations patterns (lower mutation load if compared to younger healthy controls).
evidence: The manuscript states this as a main finding based on analysis of germline and somatic mutation data.

claim: 105+/110+ individuals have lower mutation load compared to younger healthy controls.
source: The results showed that 105+/110+ are characterized by a peculiar genetic background associated with efficient DNA repair mechanisms, as evidenced by both germline data (common and rare variants) and somatic mutations patterns (lower mutation load if compared to younger healthy controls).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that 105+/110+ have lower mutation load based on somatic mutation analysis.

claim: Results were replicated in a second independent cohort of 333 Italian centenarians and 358 geographically matched controls.
source: Results were replicated in a second independent cohort of 333 Italian centenarians and 358 geographically matched controls.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the validation cohort used for replication.

claim: DNA repair and clonal haematopoiesis are crucial players for healthy aging and protection from cardiovascular events.
source: The genetics of 105+/110+ identified DNA repair and clonal haematopoiesis as crucial players for healthy aging and for the protection from cardiovascular events.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a main conclusion based on the genetic analysis.

claim: The relative risk of sibling surviving to 105 years is 35 times the chance of living to age 105 of the control population.
source: First, Sebastiani et al., 2016 showed that, considering individuals surviving to age 105 years, the relative risk of sibling surviving to 105 years is 35 times the chance of living to age 105 of the control population.
evidence: The manuscript cites Sebastiani et al., 2016 as the source of this statistic.

claim: The power to detect association with longevity is greater for centenarians versus nonagenarians samples of the same birth cohort.
source: These data suggest a more potent genetic contributions if samples are recruited in the last percentile of survival in accord with Tan et al., 2008 who reported that the power to detect association with longevity is greater for centenarians versus nonagenarians samples of the same birth cohort.
evidence: The manuscript cites Tan et al., 2008 as the source of this claim.

claim: Centenarians can be considered as a paradigm of healthy aging as they avoid or largely postpone all major age-related diseases.
source: Second, despite different definitions and opinion regarding the concept of healthy aging, the clinical and biochemical data on centenarians showed that they can be considered as a paradigm of healthy aging as they avoid or largely postpone all major age-related diseases (Andersen et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites Andersen et al., 2012 to support this characterization of centenarians.

claim: Healthy aging and exceptional longevity are deeply related.
source: Thus, healthy aging and exceptional longevity (people who live more than 100 years) are deeply related (Christensen and McGue, 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites Christensen and McGue, 2016 to support this relationship.

claim: The genetic determinants of longevity are dynamic and historically dependent.
source: In this view, the genetic determinants of longevity are dynamic and historically dependent (Giuliani et al., 2017; Giuliani et al., 2018a; Yashin et al., 2015) and, while the genetic determinants of longevity may be shared by different populations, population-specific genes are expected to play a major role (De Benedictis and Franceschi, 2006; Zeng et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies (Giuliani et al., 2017; Giuliani et al., 2018a; Yashin et al., 2015) to support this claim.

claim: Population-specific genes are expected to play a major role in longevity.
source: In this view, the genetic determinants of longevity are dynamic and historically dependent (Giuliani et al., 2017; Giuliani et al., 2018a; Yashin et al., 2015) and, while the genetic determinants of longevity may be shared by different populations, population-specific genes are expected to play a major role (De Benedictis and Franceschi, 2006; Zeng et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites De Benedictis and Franceschi, 2006 and Zeng et al., 2016 to support this claim.

source: The expansion of such mutated clones ('clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential', CHIP), has been associated to an acceleration of the atherosclerotic process, an increased risk of haematological malignancies (hazard ratio 11,1), ischemic stroke (hazard ratio 2,6), coronary heart disease (hazard ratio 2,0) and all-cause mortality (Jaiswal et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites Jaiswal et al., 2014 as the source of this association.

claim: No association was observed at the genome-wide significance level (<5*10−8) in the WGS association study.
source: First, we performed a WGS association study adding sex as covariate and considering 5,511,852 common variants (MAF >5%). No association is observed at the genome-wide significance level (<5*10−8) (Figure 2A), but significant p-values after SLIDE correction (significance at adjusted p-value 10%) are observed for STK17A and COA1 genes.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the results of the genome-wide association analysis.

claim: Significant p-values after SLIDE correction (significance at adjusted p-value 10%) are observed for STK17A and COA1 genes.
source: First, we performed a WGS association study adding sex as covariate and considering 5,511,852 common variants (MAF >5%). No association is observed at the genome-wide significance level (<5*10−8) (Figure 2A), but significant p-values after SLIDE correction (significance at adjusted p-value 10%) are observed for STK17A and COA1 genes.

claim: Five variants (rs7456688, rs10257700, rs10279856, rs69685881, and rs7805969) identified in Cohort 1 showed nominal p-values<0.05 in Cohort 2.
source: The five variants (rs7456688, rs10257700, rs10279856, rs69685881, and rs7805969) identified in Cohort 1 were evaluated for association with longevity in the validation Cohort 2. Cohort 2 includes 333 centenarians (mean age: 100.4 ± 1.4) and a group of 358 unrelated healthy individuals (controls; mean age: 60.7 ± 7.2), genotyped on the Illumina 550 k array platform. The analysis of Cohort 2 imputed genotypes (see Materials and methods) returned nominal p-values<0.05 for all the five variants, as reported in Table 1.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the replication results for these five variants.

claim: The allele frequency pattern of rs7456688-A follows a U-shaped pattern with the highest allele frequency observed for 105+/110+.
source: The pattern follows a U-shaped with the highest allele frequency observed for 105+/110+, indicating the relevant role of the variant in extreme longevity.
evidence: The manuscript describes the pattern and Figure 2C shows the allele frequencies across different cohorts.

claim: Gene-based association study identified 179 significant genes (p-values<0.01) in Cohort 1.
source: Next, we performed a gene-based association study by VEGAS2 including common variants (MAF >5%) in Cohort 1. A full list of all the 179 significant genes (p-values<0.01) is reported in Supplementary file 2, two of them (APOC3 and PPARGC1A) were already described in the GenAge database (http://genomics.senescence.info/genes/human.html), a database that includes genes identified in studies on human aging.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of significant genes identified.

evidence: The manuscript explicitly states these genes were previously identified in the GenAge database.

claim: Eight genes (STK17A, BLVRA, MYRF, DNAH7, LOC553103, PHF14, SLC22A4, TBRG4) were significant in both Cohort 1 (p-value<0.01) and Cohort 2 (p-value<0.05).
source: Among the 179 genes identified in Cohort 1 (p-value<0.01, Supplementary file 2), eight were also significant in Cohort 2 (p-value<0.05). Fisher method was applied to calculate combined-p-values for STK17A, BLVRA, MYRF, DNAH7, LOC553103, PHF14, SLC22A4, TBRG4 (p-values=2.03*10−9, 1.35*10−7, 1.83*10−7, 0.00049, 0.00146, 0.00205, 0.00154, 0.00146, respectively) and STK17A gene is the gene with the strongest association signal in Cohort 1 (p-value=8.40*10−5) and Cohort 2 (p-value=1*10−6).

source: Fisher method was applied to calculate combined-p-values for STK17A, BLVRA, MYRF, DNAH7, LOC553103, PHF14, SLC22A4, TBRG4 (p-values=2.03*10−9, 1.35*10−7, 1.83*10−7, 0.00049, 0.00146, 0.00205, 0.00154, 0.00146, respectively) and STK17A gene is the gene with the strongest association signal in Cohort 1 (p-value=8.40*10−5) and Cohort 2 (p-value=1*10−6).

claim: RiVIERA analysis identified four SNPs (rs10279856, rs3779059, rs849166, rs849175) with credible score >0.
source: We then performed a RiVIERA analysis – a tool for variant prioritization – on WGS data for inference of possible causal/regulatory variants considering SNPs located in the above-mentioned window (from chr7:43560257 to chr7:43938230) around the COA1 gene (Figure 4A). As reported in Figure 4A and SNPs, rs10279856 (in LD with the five previously reported SNPs), rs3779059, rs849166, rs849175 showed a credible score >0 (credible scores 0.261; 0.261; 0.240; 0.236 respectively).

evidence: The manuscript explicitly states these SNPs are eQTLs based on GTEx data.

source: First, in order to exploit the richness of our WGS data set, we considered 9,303,614 rare variants (minor allele frequency <1% in both 105+/110+ and CTRL) for association with longevity using a gene-burden association test (SKAT-O). The top hit was a region located on chromosome 17 (49,230,046 bp to 49,238,995 bp) containing NME1 gene (p-value=6 *10−5).

The complete list of genes identified is reported in Supplementary file 11. claim: 147 somatic mutations were identified in 80 individuals.
source: The analysis of somatic mutations was performed considering those individuals whose cell count is not compromised as suggested by a recent paper (Jaiswal et al., 2014). For this analysis, 79 105+/110+ and 31 controls have been considered. We identified 147 somatic mutations in 80 individuals.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of somatic mutations identified.

source: By comparing the total number of somatic mutations between controls and 105+/110+ considering the seven analysed genes altogether (DNMT3A, TP53, ASXL1, TET2, SF3B1, PPM1D, JAK2), we found significant differences between the groups (Mann-Whitney p-value=0.00125) where 105+/110+ have a reduce burden of mutations, the median number of mutations being one for 105+/110+ and two for controls.

claim: 105+/110+ have a reduced burden of somatic mutations with median number of mutations being one for 105+/110+ and two for controls.

In this case, the total prevalence considering all seven genes was 10.13% for 105+/110+ and 0% for controls which was not statistically significant (Fisher's test p-value=0.1025).

claim: No significant differences in polygenic risk scores (PRS) for CVD were found between 105+/110+ and controls (p-value>0.05).
source: Moreover, to check the presence of cardiovascular risk variants in 105+/110+ we calculated the five most recent polygenic risk scores (PRS) for CVD in CTRL and 105+/110+ to see if 105+/110+ are characterized by lower PRS than controls. We calculated PRS according to Natarajan et al., 2017 (67 SNVs), Nelson et al., 2017, UK Biobank CardioMetabolic Consortium CHD Working Group et al., 2019 (300 SNVs), van der Harst and Verweij, 2018 (661 SNVs), Khera et al., 2018 (6630150 SNVs). No significant differences were found (p-value>0.05) (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the lack of significant differences in PRS.

claim: STK17A is involved in DNA damage response and positive regulation of apoptotic process.
source: STK17A is involved in DNA damage response and positive regulation of apoptotic process (Sanjo et al., 1998) and regulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) metabolic process.

source: SNP rs7805969-A allele (located in STK17A/COA1 region) was found to be associated to systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) in a population from Southern Brazil (da Silva Fonseca et al., 2013), and a reduced expression of SKT17A has been observed during the active phase of SLE disease (Sandrin-Garcia et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites Sandrin-Garcia et al., 2009 for this observation.

claim: Genetic variants in STK17A may maintain DNA damage responses in 105+/110+, favoring healthy aging.
source: In this model, genetic variants in STK17A may maintain DNA damage responses in 105+/110+, favoring healthy aging.

claim: COA1 gene is a component of the MITRAC complex that regulates cytochrome c oxidase assembly.

source: PLEKHG4 is associated with Spinocerebellar ataxia, a neurodegenerative disease affecting cerebellar Purkinje cells.
